titulo.texto: The Constitution of 1917 and González Camarena’s Mural

frase_gancho.texto: In this mural, an eagle dictates the Constitution to Carranza: this is how González Camarena imagined the birth of the law of nineteen seventeen.

puente_narrativo.texto: When you finish here, head to the Alcázar, the part of the castle that was home to emperors and presidents.

guion_corto.texto: When Venustiano Carranza opened the Constituent Congress on December first, nineteen sixteen, he was not trying to write a new constitution. He wanted to reform the one of eighteen fifty-seven. But the deputies gathered in the Iturbide Theater of Querétaro added social rights. Article Three established secular education. Article Twenty-Seven dealt with land and the nation’s resources. Article One Hundred Twenty-Three dealt with workers’ rights. The Constitution was promulgated on February fifth, nineteen seventeen. Jorge González Camarena imagined it this way in this mural of nineteen sixty-seven: Carranza writes, and an eagle, representing the nation, dictates to him.

guion_largo.texto:
In nineteen fifteen, Venustiano Carranza announced that he wanted to call a congress to give the country a new fundamental law. He could only do so after the Convention of Aguascalientes, in nineteen fourteen, split the Constitutionalists from the Villistas and Zapatistas, and after he defeated the latter. The call for the congress was published in the autumn of nineteen sixteen. The Constituent Congress was installed on December first, nineteen sixteen, in the Iturbide Theater of Querétaro, today the Theater of the Republic. The deputies had two months to approve the text.

The draft that Carranza presented at the first session had been written by Luis Manuel Rojas and José Natividad Macías. Carranza explained that it was based on the liberal spirit of the Constitution of eighteen fifty-seven. That is the one Siqueiros paints trampled underfoot in his [mural on Porfirian rule](chap_09_mural_siqueiros). Even so, the Congress went further. According to the Institute of Historical Research of UNAM, the deputies added a social vision in Articles Three, Five, Twenty-Seven and One Hundred Twenty-Three. The committee that reviewed the draft, with Francisco J. Múgica, Enrique Colunga and Luis G. Monzón among its members, pushed for those changes.

There were two main groups. The renovators, such as Macías, Rojas, Alfonso Cravioto and Félix Palavicini, had been deputies under Madero. The radicals, such as Francisco Múgica and Cándido Aguilar, pushed for deeper social change. Both groups belonged to the same faction and often voted together. Only supporters of Constitutionalism could take part. Military chiefs and sympathizers of the Villistas and Zapatistas were left out. That is why Emiliano Zapata and Francisco Villa were not in the theater in Querétaro.

There are three best-known provisions. Article Three established secular, compulsory and free education in public schools. Article Twenty-Seven dealt with the ownership of land and subsoil resources, and recognized the nation’s sovereignty over them. Its main author was Pastor Rouaix. Article One Hundred Twenty-Three, which Macías drafted, recognized the right to strike and to organize in unions. It also established a minimum wage and a maximum workday of eight hours. Two more articles marked the century: Article One Hundred Fifteen, which established the free municipality, and Article One Hundred Thirty, on relations between the State and the Church.

It is often said that this was the first constitution in the world to recognize social rights. The Secretariat of Public Education presents it that way, and Rouaix, one of its authors, held the same view. Later constitutions, such as the German one of nineteen nineteen, included similar labor provisions. It is best to put it carefully: it was one of the pioneers and a model for others.

The Congress met until January thirty-first, nineteen seventeen. The Constitution was promulgated on February fifth and took effect on May first of the same year. It has one hundred thirty-seven articles. The historian Álvaro Matute calculated that it has undergone close to seven hundred amendments, which makes it hard to read. Carranza, born in Cuatro Ciénegas, Coahuila, in eighteen fifty-nine, did not live to see the long institutional path it followed: in nineteen twenty his opponents rose up against him, he evacuated the capital, and he was assassinated in Tlaxcalantongo, Puebla, on May twentieth.

The mural in front of you was painted by Jorge González Camarena in nineteen sixty-seven, fifty years after the promulgation. It measures five meters and ten centimeters high by four meters and ninety centimeters wide, and it is acrylic on wood covered with cloth. It shows Carranza writing. An eagle, representing the nation, dictates to him. It is an allegory: the actual text was the work of many deputies, not only Carranza.

This same artist painted another mural in the museum, The Fusion of Two Cultures. It tells of the origin of the Mexican nation in the clash between the Nahua and Spanish worlds. That mural opens the story that this one comes to close.

texto.pregunta: Myth: Emiliano Zapata and Francisco Villa signed the Constitution of 1917 alongside Venustiano Carranza.
texto.respuesta: Reality: They did not take part in the Congress of Querétaro. Only supporters of Constitutionalism could attend, and military chiefs and sympathizers of the Villistas and Zapatistas were excluded. The issues of land and labor were indeed debated, in Articles Twenty-Seven and One Hundred Twenty-Three.
